title: What Must a Gentile Do to Be Saved?
paragraphs:
What Must a Gentile Do to Be Saved?
The Question That Changed Eternity—and Why the Answer Still Shocks Religious People Today
There is a question that has haunted humanity for thousands of years.
What must I do to be saved?
Every human heart eventually arrives there.
The businessman hiding anxiety behind achievements.
The mother carrying guilt she never speaks about.
The addict promising tomorrow will be different.
The churchgoer wondering if they have done enough.
The skeptic secretly asking what happens after death.
Because beneath every accomplishment, every distraction, every failure, every victory, there remains a deeper question:
How can a sinful person stand before a holy God and live?
For the Gentiles—the nations outside ethnic Israel—this question carried another burden.
Could they truly belong to God's family?
Or would they always remain outsiders looking through the window of a covenant they never inherited?
The answer became one of the most important controversies in the entire New Testament.
And the conclusion changed the world forever.
And if you understand it correctly, it may change your life today.
They inherited the promises given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
People who had spent their lives bowing before false gods.
People who knew nothing of the Law of Moses.
People whose pasts were stained with paganism, immorality, and spiritual darkness.
Yet the Holy Spirit began transforming them.
And many religious people became uncomfortable.
Some insisted that faith in Jesus was not enough.
They argued that Gentiles must first become Jews.
They must keep the Mosaic Law.
Only then could they be fully accepted.
The debate became so serious that the apostles gathered in Jerusalem to settle the matter once and for all.
The event is commonly called the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15.
There, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the apostles answered the question that still matters today:
What are the requirements for Gentiles to receive salvation?
Simon Peter stood before the assembly and reminded them what God had already done among the Gentiles.

“Why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” (Acts 15:10–11)
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
Something earned by neither effort nor religious performance.
Everyone is saved the same way.
The apostle Paul would later write:
τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
"For by grace you have been saved through faith."
Yet the Jerusalem Council did provide instructions for Gentile believers.
This is where many readers become confused.
"...abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood."
Some mistakenly assume these were conditions for salvation.
The apostles had already concluded that salvation comes by grace through faith.
These instructions were given for fellowship, holiness, and unity between Jewish and Gentile believers.
They addressed practical issues causing division in the early church.
The requirements did not create salvation.
"God accepts you through Christ, therefore obey."
Religion works from earth toward heaven.
The Gospel comes from heaven toward earth.
When Jesus hung upon the cross, He cried out:
The debt of sin was satisfied by Christ Himself.
This truth reaches all the way back to Abraham.
Long before circumcision became the sign of the covenant.
And God counted it to him as righteousness.
Paul builds his entire argument in Romans upon this foundation.
Salvation has always been God's work.
And this is where our story becomes deeply personal.
Because many people today still live like the debate of Acts 15 was never settled.
They fear they are never good enough.
Every failure becomes evidence against them.
"God cannot possibly love someone like you."
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Gospel is the story of scandal becoming grace.
It is the story of prostitutes becoming worshipers.
The Gospel is not about good people climbing toward God.
It is about God descending toward ruined people through Jesus Christ.
That is why Gentile salvation matters.
Because most of us reading this are Gentiles.
"But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ."
Not brought near by religious credentials.
Perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
Your failures may still haunt you.
You may think you've wandered too far.
But Jesus specializes in bringing distant people home.
The cross was never built for perfect people.
The empty tomb was never meant for the deserving.
It was meant for the hopeless.
And salvation remains exactly what it was in Acts 15.
Place your faith in Jesus Christ.
Trust His death for your sins.
Trust His resurrection for your justification.
Receive the grace He freely offers.
Have you ever struggled with feeling like you had to earn God's acceptance?
Because the greatest miracle is not that sinners find God.
It is that God came searching for sinners.
